warmup.q: On 4 November your risk team moves merchant 1 from the LOW to the HIGH risk tier, and the warehouse updates the merchant's one row. On 10 November finance reruns the report "captured volume by risk tier, 1 to 3 November". Where does merchant 1's volume from those three days land?
options: Under LOW, the tier merchant 1 had on those days
Under HIGH, the tier the row says today
Split between LOW and HIGH by date
Nowhere: the update detaches the old payments
warmup.why: The report joins each payment to the merchant's row, and there is only one row, which now says HIGH. Overwriting a dimension row (type 1) rewrites history: the same report over the same days gives a different answer after the change. In this lesson's demo the HIGH tier's volume for those days grows by 97%. LOW, the tempting answer, is what you only get if the warehouse kept the old version as its own row, which is type 2.

sections.h: Analytics asks about events, so the warehouse stores events
sections.html:
The first lesson of the What data systems are for track split data work in two. Operational work, also called OLTP (online transaction processing), touches a few rows by key, thousands of times a second: authorize this payment, read that merchant. Analytical work, OLAP (online analytical processing), scans millions of rows to answer a few questions a day: how much did each merchant category capture on weekends, per week, this quarter? The lessons before this one built the machinery for the second kind: files, columns, shuffles and joins. This lesson is about the shape of the tables that machinery reads.

Start with the tables you already have. The payments service keeps raw_payments: id, merchant, card country, currency, amount, status and a timestamp. The onboarding service keeps raw_merchants: name, category code, risk tier and country. A small lookup table, raw_mcc, turns a merchant category code (in this track, made-up codes from 5000 to 5019) into a name such as Travel. Each fact is stored once, which is right for writes.

Version 1: run the analyst's question on those tables, in the production database. It works once, and then it breaks three ways. A row store reads every column of a row to use three of them, as the Storage track's column-store lesson measured. The scan competes with checkouts for the same disks and memory. And every analyst rewrites the date logic (is this a weekend? which fiscal quarter?) in every query, a little differently each time.

Version 2: copy the data into a separate analytical store, reshaped around the questions. The shape that has served for 30 years comes from Ralph Kimball's dimensional modelling, and it's called a star schema. In the middle sits a fact table: one row per event, at a grain you declare before anything else. Here the grain is one row per payment. A fact row holds measures, the numbers you add up (amount_cents), and foreign keys into the dimension tables around it. A dimension table describes who, what, where and when, in as many columns as analysts want. dim_merchant holds the name, the category already looked up, the risk tier and the country. dim_date holds one row per day with its weekday, a weekend flag, the month and the quarter, so nobody computes a weekend by hand again. Small attributes with no table of their own, such as status, stay on the fact row; Kimball calls them degenerate dimensions.

The shape follows from the work. Facts are many and narrow: millions or billions of rows of keys and numbers, written once and never changed. Dimensions are few and wide: hundreds or thousands of rows of text. A query filters and groups by dimension columns and sums fact columns. In the Try it, a million payments become a fact table of 1,000,000 rows and 7 columns, next to a 7-row date dimension and a 500-row merchant dimension, and the analyst's question becomes two joins and a group-by.

sections.h: Star, snowflake or one big table: decide when the joins happen
sections.html:
A dimension can be stored three ways. The difference is when the joins happen.

The star keeps each dimension flat. dim_merchant carries the category name itself, copied onto every merchant in that category, so any merchant attribute is one join away from a fact. The lookup from code to category ran once, when the dimension was built.

A snowflake schema normalizes the dimensions instead. dim_merchant keeps only the category code, a dim_category table names it, and a dim_category_group might sit above that. The diagram grows branches, hence the name, which is older than the company called Snowflake and unrelated to it. Each dimension fact is now stored once, the same argument as normalization in the relational model track's schema-design lesson. The cost is one more join per level in every query, for tables of a few thousand rows where the saving is a few kilobytes. Analysts mostly prefer the star, and so should you.

One big table (OBT) goes the other way: it copies every dimension column onto every fact row, so the joins happen once, when the table is written, and every query scans one table. In a row store that would be wasteful: the merchant's name repeated on every one of its payments. In a column store it's cheap, because a column with 500 distinct names compresses to small codes, as the Storage track's column-store lesson showed with dictionary and run-length encoding. In the Try it, the star's Parquet files take 10.8 MB and an 18-column big table takes 14.6 MB. The same question takes 8 ms on the star and 7 ms on the big table: two hash joins against 7 and 500 rows cost almost nothing.

The price of one big table is change. Facts are history and don't change; dimension attributes do, and some turn out to be wrong. If merchant 7's category was wrong all along, the star fixes one row of a 500-row table. The big table has to rewrite all 1,958 of merchant 7's payments, and since the file is stored in date order, those rows sit in all 9 of its row groups: in practice the whole file. So keep the star as the source, and build a big table from it as derived data when one dashboard needs it, which you can rebuild whenever a dimension changes.

Copying 11 dimension columns onto every fact row cost about 35% more disk, far less than the raw text would suggest, because each copied column has at most 500 distinct values and compresses to small codes. The query was no slower on the star: the two dimensions fit in hash tables of a few kilobytes. The correction is where the designs differ. The star changes one row; the big table has 1,958 rows to change, and the min/max statistics of merchant_id can't rule out a single row group, because every day's payments include merchant 7. sections.h: When a dimension changes, decide what history means
sections.html:
Facts don't change, but dimensions do. A merchant moves to the HIGH risk tier, changes category, moves country. Every such change forces a question that sounds philosophical and is really about money: should last month's payments count under the merchant's old tier or its new one? Kimball calls a dimension whose rows change now and then a slowly changing dimension (SCD), and numbers the answers.

Type 1 overwrites: UPDATE dim_merchant SET risk_tier = 'HIGH' WHERE merchant_id = 1. There's one row per merchant and no history, so every report from then on groups old payments by the new tier. That's right for a correction (a misspelled name) and wrong for anything that changed in the world. In the Try it, 50 merchants move to HIGH on 4 November. Rerun the report for 1 to 3 November afterwards, and the HIGH tier's captured volume for those days grows from 2.19 billion cents to 4.31 billion, plus 97%. Same days, same payments, twice the money in the tier, and an auditor comparing the two runs would ask what happened.

Type 2 adds a row. The merchant's current row is closed: its valid_to becomes the day of the change and is_current becomes false. A new row is inserted with the new tier, valid from that day. Each version gets its own surrogate key (merchant_key), a number that means nothing outside the warehouse, while merchant_id stays the durable business key that ties the versions together. A fact row stores the surrogate key of the version that was valid when its payment happened. Payments from before the change join to the LOW version and payments after it to the HIGH version, and no query has to know any dates. The stepper walks through one change.

Two details decide whether type 2 stays correct. The fact load must look up the version that was valid on the payment's day, not the current one, because payments arrive late: a payment from 3 November that lands on 6 November belongs to the old version. And applying the same change twice must not create a second version, because batch jobs get retried (lesson 13 is about exactly that).

Type 2 answers "as it was". Sometimes finance wants "as it is": all of a merchant's history under today's tier. You get it by going from the fact's version to the durable merchant_id, then to the current version. Kimball's types 6 and 7 make that cheap by keeping a current-value column on every version, or a second, durable key on the fact row. The rest of the catalogue is smaller. Type 0 never changes an attribute (a merchant's onboarding date). Type 3 keeps one previous value in an extra column (previous_tier), enough for one change. Type 4 moves fast-changing attributes into a small dimension of their own. Spark 4.3's Declarative Pipelines can maintain a type 2 table for you (CREATE FLOW ... AS AUTO CDC INTO), into a table format that supports row-level changes, such as Iceberg; lesson 12 shows how such changes are written.

try.title: Overwrite the tier, or keep its history
steps: Run ScdDemo. It builds the star, moves 50 merchants to HIGH on 4 November in two copies of the merchant dimension (type 1 and type 2), and asks both for the HIGH tier's captured volume on 1 to 3 November.
Before reading: which copy will change its answer about days that were already over?
Look at the two versions of merchant 1. Where does one end and the next begin?

code.title: ScdDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l10.demo /** * On 2026-11-04 the risk team moves 50 merchants (ids 1, 11, 21, ... 491) to the HIGH tier. The * same change is applied to two copies of the star: type 1 (overwrite the dimension row) and * type 2 (close the old version, add a new one). Then both answer last week's question: how much * captured volume came from HIGH-risk merchants on 1 to 3 November, before the change? */ fun main() { duck().use { c -> rawTables(c, 1_000_000) buildStar(c) c.run("CREATE TABLE moved AS SELECT CAST(10 * k + 1 AS INTEGER) AS merchant_id FROM range(50) t(k)") println("before the change: " + c.rows("SELECT risk_tier, count(*) FROM dim_merchant WHERE merchant_id IN (SELECT merchant_id FROM moved) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1") .joinToString { "${it[1]} ${it[0]}" } + " merchants are moving to HIGH") // type 1: overwrite. One row per merchant, no history c.run("CREATE TABLE dim_merchant_t1 AS SELECT * FROM dim_merchant") c.run("UPDATE dim_merchant_t1 SET risk_tier = 'HIGH' WHERE merchant_id IN (SELECT merchant_id FROM moved)") // type 2: close the current version and add a new one with a new surrogate key c.run("CREATE TABLE dim_merchant_t2 AS SELECT * FROM dim_merchant") c.run(""" INSERT INTO dim_merchant_t2 SELECT CAST(500 + row_number() OVER (ORDER BY merchant_id) AS INTEGER), merchant_id, merchant_name, mcc, category, 'HIGH', country, DATE '2026-11-04', DATE '9999-12-31', true FROM dim_merchant WHERE sections.h: Warehouses broadcast the dimensions and prune the facts
sections.html:
A star query always has the same shape: one huge table, a few small ones, filters on the small ones and sums over the huge one. Analytical engines are built around that shape. The storage half was the Storage track's column-store lesson: columns stored apart, compressed, with a min/max zone map per chunk, and Snowflake's micro-partitions as the cloud-sized version. This section is the join half.

Start from lesson 7's two distributed joins. A sort-merge join would shuffle a billion fact rows across the network by merchant_key to meet 500 merchant rows. A broadcast hash join sends the small side to every machine instead, builds a hash table from it there, and streams the fact rows past it where they already sit. For a star that is almost always the right plan: every machine gets every dimension, and the fact table never moves. The Snowflake paper (SIGMOD 2016) describes star schemas in exactly those terms: a small broadcast dimension joined to a large partitioned fact table, with little network traffic.

The second trick runs the filter backwards. The query asks for weekends and HIGH-risk merchants. Once the engine has built the hash tables from the filtered dimensions, it knows every date_key and merchant_key that can possibly join: two dates and 50 merchants. It turns them into a filter on the fact table's scan, at run time, and the zone maps then skip every chunk whose date_key range holds no weekend. In the Try it, DuckDB's plan over 4 million payments shows that filter as date_key IN (20261101, 20261107) plus a list of merchant keys. The scan reads 11 of 33 row groups and hands 47,775 rows to the join. With the optimization switched off, it reads all 33 row groups and hands over 1,599,756 rows for the join to throw away. Spark calls the same idea dynamic partition pruning, and the Snowflake paper describes pruning files during a hash join from the keys its build side produced.

The three big cloud warehouses run star queries the same way, with different knobs:

  • Snowflake keeps tables as immutable columnar files on S3, runs queries on elastic virtual warehouses with local SSD caches, and keeps the file lists and their statistics in a separate metadata service. It prunes files from the WHERE clause before the query starts, and from the join while it runs.
  • BigQuery runs Dremel-style execution over columnar storage, with the shuffle held in memory. Google's own guidance is that star schemas already suit analytics well, and that denormalizing them further may not make queries much faster.
  • Redshift is a cluster in which every node holds a slice of every table, and you choose how rows are spread. KEY distribution puts rows with the same key on the same slice, so a fact table and a large dimension distributed on their join key meet without moving. ALL keeps a full copy of a table on every node: a broadcast decided at load time. The default, AUTO, starts small tables as ALL and changes them as they grow, and AWS's documentation adds that copying a small dimension at query time is cheap, so forcing ALL rarely pays.

What you control is the same everywhere: keep dimensions small, and store facts sorted or clustered by the column most queries filter through, usually the date. The engine does the rest.

try.title: Watch a dimension filter reach the fact table
steps: Run StarJoinDemo. It builds a star over 4 million payments, stored in date order, and asks for the captured weekend volume of HIGH-risk merchants. The filters are only on dim_date and dim_merchant. It prints what the scan of fact_payment did, then runs the query again with DuckDB's join_filter_pushdown optimizer switched off.
Predict how many of the fact table's 33 row groups the first run reads. Two of the seven days are weekend days.
Where did the list of 50 merchant keys come from? The query never mentions them.

code.title: StarJoinDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l10.demo /** * How an engine runs a star join. The fact table (4 million payments, stored in date order) is * joined to two small dimensions with filters on the dimensions only. Prints what DuckDB's scan of * the fact table did: the filter the join pushed into it at run time, the row groups it read, and * the rows it produced. Then the same query with that run-time filter switched off. */ fun main() { duck().use { c -> rawTables(c, 4_000_000) buildStar(c) val query = """ SELECT sum(f.amount_cents) FROM fact_payment f JOIN dim_date d ON d.date_key = f.date_key JOIN dim_merchant m ON m.merchant_key = f.merchant_key WHERE d.is_weekend AND m.risk_tier = 'HIGH' AND f.status = 'CAPTURED'""" val answer = c.rows(query).first()[0] println("captured weekend volume of HIGH-risk merchants: %,d cents".format(answer)) report(c, query, "with run-time join filters (the default)") c.run("SET disabled_optimizers = 'join_filter_pushdown'") report(c, query, "with join_filter_pushdown switched off") } } /** Prints the lines of `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` that describe the scan of `fact_payment`. */ private fun report(c: java.sql.Connection, query: String, label: String) { val plan = c.rows("EXPLAIN ANALYZE $query").first()[1].toString() // the plan is drawn as boxes; keep the left-most box of each line, which holds the fact scan val lines = plan.lines().map { it.substringAfter("│").substringBefore("│").trim() } val start = lines.indexOfFirst { it == "Table: memory.main.fact_payment" } val box = lines.drop(start).takeWhile { it.isNotEmpty() && !it.startsWith("╰") } println("$label, the fact table's scan:") box.filter { "Filters" in it || "optional" in it || "Row Groups" in it || "rows" in it || it.startsWith("(") } .forEach { println(" " + it.replace(Regex("\\s+\\d+(\\.\\d+)?(µs|ms|s)$"), "")) } }

The query only filtered the dimensions, yet the fact scan received filters on date_key and merchant_key: the values that survived the dimension filters, collected from the join's hash tables while the query ran. (PRF is a second, probabilistic form of the same filter, a Bloom-like test DuckDB can apply cheaply per row.) Because the fact table is stored in date order, the zone maps of 22 row groups showed no weekend date, and those row groups were never read. Without the run-time filter, the scan read every row group and passed 33 times as many rows to the join. The plan lines are cut to the fact table's scan.

analogy: A fact table is a bookkeeper's journal: one line per transaction, in the order they happened, with an account number, a date and an amount, and nothing else. The dimensions are the card files on the desk beside it: one card per account with its owner, branch and category, one card per day with its weekday and whether the bank was open. To answer "what did travel accounts spend on weekends?" you read the journal once and look at each line's cards. A type 2 change is filing a new card when an account changes hands and stamping the old one "valid until 4 November", instead of crossing out the old owner's name, so last month's lines still lead to last month's owner. The analogy breaks at scale: a bookkeeper fetches cards one at a time, while a warehouse copies the whole card file to every machine, filters it first, and uses what's left to skip whole pages of the journal without reading them.
world: Your Oracle ledger is the operational side: normalized, row by row, tuned for authorizations and settlement updates. When finance asks for captured volume by merchant risk tier, resist the reporting index on the ledger and the eight-join view. Load a star in the warehouse your data team runs instead: fact_payment at one row per payment (or per settlement line, if that's the question), a dim_merchant kept as type 2 from the onboarding service's change events on Kafka, and a dim_date that knows your fiscal calendar and the card networks' processing holidays. Your idempotency keys have a cousin here. The fact load skips payment ids it already has and the SCD job skips changes equal to the current version, so a retried Temporal activity or a replayed Kafka partition adds nothing.
mistake: The common mistake is updating dimension rows in place for attributes that change in the world, because the operational schema works that way: the merchants table has one row per merchant, so the warehouse copy does too. Nothing fails. Then a quarter's report is rerun and the numbers move, or the HIGH tier's volume jumps after a re-tiering and nobody can tell whether fraud grew or the tiers changed. The fix is to decide what history means for each attribute before the first load: overwrite for corrections (type 1), new versions for real changes (type 2), surrogate keys on the fact rows so each payment keeps the version it was made under. Then load facts by looking up the version valid on the event's day, so late payments land right, and make both loads skip what they have already written.

compare.title: The analyst's question on a star and on one big table

a.label: Star schema
a.title: two joins against small dimensions
a.html: SELECT m.category, d.is_weekend, count(*), sum(f.amount_cents) FROM fact_payment f JOIN dim_date d ON d.date_key = f.date_key JOIN dim_merchant m ON m.merchant_key = f.merchant_key WHERE f.status = 'CAPTURED' GROUP BY m.category, d.is_weekend;

b.label: One big table
b.title: the joins were done when the table was written
b.html: SELECT category, is_weekend, count(*), sum(amount_cents) FROM payments_obt WHERE status = 'CAPTURED' GROUP BY category, is_weekend;

compare.note: Both return the same eight rows, and in a column store both read only the columns they name: category, is_weekend, status and amount_cents on the left, as two small joins plus four fact columns. The right one is shorter to write and skips the joins, which matters little when the dimensions fit in a few kilobytes of hash table, as in the demo (8 ms against 7 ms). The real difference is maintenance: the star corrects a merchant in one dimension row, while the big table rewrites every payment of that merchant. Keep the star as the source and derive a big table when a dashboard needs it.

worked.title: Design a star for the settlement report

steps.say: Declare the grain first, in one sentence, because every other choice follows from it. The settlement report sums what each merchant is paid out, so the event is a settlement line: one captured payment inside one payout batch.
steps.code:
grain: one row per settlement line
       (one captured payment in one payout batch to one merchant)

steps.say: List what analysts filter and group by (dimensions) and what they add up (measures). Things that identify a line but describe nothing, such as the batch id, stay on the fact row as degenerate dimensions.
steps.code:
dimensions: date (payout day), merchant (type 2: tier and category change),
            card network, currency
measures:   gross_cents, fee_cents, net_cents
degenerate: payout_batch_id, payment_id

steps.say: Write the fact table: surrogate keys to the dimensions, the degenerate ids, and the measures. Nothing descriptive goes here.
steps.code: CREATE TABLE fact_settlement_line ( date_key INTEGER NOT NULL, -- yyyymmdd of the payout day merchant_key INTEGER NOT NULL, -- the merchant version valid that day network_key SMALLINT NOT NULL, currency_key SMALLINT NOT NULL, payout_batch_id BIGINT NOT NULL, -- degenerate dimension payment_id BIGINT NOT NULL, gross_cents BIGINT NOT NULL, fee_cents BIGINT NOT NULL, net_cents BIGINT NOT NULL );

steps.say: Check each measure for additivity. net_cents adds up across every dimension. A merchant's outstanding balance would not: you can sum balances across merchants on one day, never across days. Kimball calls that semi-additive, and it belongs in a separate daily snapshot fact table, one row per merchant per day.
steps.code: SELECT d.month, m.risk_tier, sum(f.net_cents) -- additive: fine across days FROM fact_settlement_line f JOIN dim_date d ON d.date_key = f.date_key JOIN dim_merchant m ON m.merchant_key = f.merchant_key GROUP BY d.month, m.risk_tier; -- a balance is semi-additive: sum it per day, never over days -- fact_merchant_balance_daily (date_key, merchant_key, balance_cents)

lab.title: Build a payments star and keep its history
steps: Run the tests. All nine fail on TODOs. Each test class opens an in-memory DuckDB database, loads the raw tables from RawData (the week from Sunday 2026-11-01, 500 merchants) and creates the empty star with the given createTables and loadDates. Read RawData.kt and createTables first: they define every table and column.
Write loadMerchants: one INSERT ... SELECT that joins raw_merchants to raw_mcc, so the category lives in the dimension, with keys 1 to 500 in merchant_id order.
Write loadFacts: join each raw payment to the merchant version whose validity covers the payment's day, skip payment ids that are already loaded, and return the number of rows inserted.
Write capturedByCategoryAndDayType: two joins, a filter and a group-by. StarSchemaTest compares your answer with one computed in plain Kotlin from the raw rows.

Write applyScd2 and volumeByTier. Scd2Test loads 1 to 3 November, moves merchant 7 to HIGH and merchant 42 to a new category on 4 November, sends merchant 8 again unchanged, then loads the rest of the week and one payment from 3 November that arrived late.
Run until all nine pass. Then look at the test of as-was against as-is and decide which one a quarterly finance report should use.
hints: Keys in order: CAST(row_number() OVER (ORDER BY m.merchant_id) AS INTEGER). The date key of a timestamp: CAST(strftime(p.created_at, '%Y%m%d') AS INTEGER).

The version valid on a day: m.valid_from <= CAST(p.created_at AS DATE) AND CAST(p.created_at AS DATE) < m.valid_to. Skipping loaded rows: WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fact_payment f WHERE f.payment_id = p.payment_id). executeUpdate returns the row count.

In applyScd2, set c.autoCommit = false, then for each change read the current version (WHERE merchant_id = ? AND is_current). Skip it if tier and mcc are equal. Otherwise UPDATE ... SET valid_to = ?, is_current = false WHERE merchant_key = ?, and INSERT ... SELECT (SELECT max(merchant_key) FROM dim_merchant) + 1, ... copying the other columns from the old version. RawData.category(mcc) gives the new category. Commit at the end, roll back on an exception.
As is: join the fact's version v, then dim_merchant cur ON cur.merchant_id = v.merchant_id AND cur.is_current, and group by cur.risk_tier.

drill.title: A type 2 change in two statements
drill.prompt: From memory, write the SQL that moves merchant 42 to the HIGH tier from 2026-11-04 as a type 2 change in dim_merchant(merchant_key, merchant_id, merchant_name, mcc, category, risk_tier, country, valid_from, valid_to, is_current). Then write the join that gives each fact row the version valid on its payment's day, when loading from raw_payments(payment_id, merchant_id, created_at, ...).

answer.html: -- 1. close the current version (inside one transaction with step 2) UPDATE dim_merchant SET valid_to = DATE '2026-11-04', is_current = false WHERE merchant_id = 42 AND is_current; -- 2. add the new version with the next surrogate key INSERT INTO dim_merchant SELECT (SELECT max(merchant_key) FROM dim_merchant) + 1, merchant_id, merchant_name, mcc, category, 'HIGH', country, DATE '2026-11-04', DATE '9999-12-31', true FROM dim_merchant WHERE merchant_id = 42 AND valid_to = DATE '2026-11-04'; -- 3. a fact row gets the version valid on its day, not the current one SELECT p.payment_id, m.merchant_key FROM raw_payments p JOIN dim_merchant m ON m.merchant_id = p.merchant_id AND m.valid_from <= CAST(p.created_at AS DATE) AND CAST(p.created_at AS DATE) < m.valid_to;

recap: Analytical queries scan many events and group them by descriptive attributes, so a warehouse stores a fact table of events at a declared grain (measures plus keys) and dimension tables of who, what, where and when.

A star keeps dimensions flat, one join each. A snowflake normalizes them into more tables and more joins. One big table pre-joins everything: column compression makes it cheap to store, and dimension corrections make it expensive to keep.

Type 1 overwrites and rewrites history. Type 2 closes the current version and adds a new one with a new surrogate key, and each fact keeps the key of the version valid on its day. Type 3 keeps one previous value; types 6 and 7 add current values or a durable key for as-is reports.
Load facts by looking up the version valid on the event's day, so late events land right, and make the fact load and the SCD job idempotent.

Warehouses broadcast small dimensions, push the keys that survive the dimension filters into the fact scan at run time, and skip chunks by their zone maps. Redshift lets you choose KEY or ALL distribution; Snowflake and BigQuery decide for you.

explain.prompt: Explain to a finance analyst why the warehouse keeps two rows for merchant 7, and how a report about last week still puts its payments under the tier they had then.
explain.answer: Merchant 7 changed tier on 4 November, from LOW to HIGH. If we had simply overwritten its one row, every report would now show all of its past payments as HIGH-risk, including reports about days before the change, and rerunning last week's report would give a different number. So instead the warehouse keeps versions. The old row is closed: it says LOW, valid from 1 November until 4 November. A new row says HIGH, valid from 4 November with no end yet. Each version has its own warehouse key, and when a payment is loaded it gets the key of the version that was valid on the day it was made, even if the payment arrives late. A report that joins payments to merchants on that key therefore sees each payment with the tier it had at the time: last week's payments stay under LOW. If you want the other view, all of the merchant's history under today's tier, we can join through the merchant's id to its current version instead. Both answers are right; they answer different questions, and the report should say which one it uses.

deeper.html:
Kimball's catalogue goes well beyond this lesson. Facts come in three kinds of table: transaction facts (one row per event, like ours), periodic snapshots (one row per merchant per day with a balance), and accumulating snapshots (one row per payment, updated as it moves through authorization, capture, settlement and payout). Measures are additive, semi-additive (balances: sum across merchants, never across days) or non-additive (ratios: recompute from their parts). Conformed dimensions are dimensions shared by several fact tables, such as one dim_merchant used by payments, disputes and payouts, so their reports can be lined up. A factless fact table records that something happened with no measure at all, such as a merchant being onboarded.

Databases have started to enforce type 2 rules themselves. PostgreSQL 18 added temporal keys: a primary key declared as PRIMARY KEY (merchant_id, valid_during WITHOUT OVERLAPS) on a range column refuses two versions of a merchant whose validity overlaps, the invariant the lab's last test checks by hand. Spark 4.3's Declarative Pipelines generate the close-and-insert logic from a change feed (AUTO CDC), and dbt has snapshots for the same job.

Designing Data-Intensive Applications (2nd edition) covers star and snowflake schemas and one big table in chapter 3, and column storage and query execution for these workloads in chapter 4. For the vendors, read the Snowflake paper's sections on pruning, Redshift's guide to distribution and sort keys, and the Dremel paper for how BigQuery runs nested columnar data.
